You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Put a frog in the toilet
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Is a frog visibly present inside the toilet bowl?
node.criteria: Pass if the image clearly shows a frog within the toilet bowl; fail if the bowl is visible and no frog is inside it; unknown if the bowl or its contents cannot be assessed reliably.
node.binding: Assess the frog’s placement relative to the toilet bowl in the image, using the toilet in the input image as the reference. A frog elsewhere does not satisfy this check.

node_traces.evidence: A frog is clearly visible inside the toilet bowl in the edited image.

fulfillment: The node’s criterion is too coarse: it treats any clearly visible frog inside the bowl as complete, while the edited image also shows frogs on the raised lid and floor, so the requested placement has progressed but is not unambiguously fulfilled across the edit. Preserve the existing completion requirement, but make the decision explicitly compare the edited image with the source and distinguish a frog actually within the bowl from frogs merely near/on the toilet; assess whether the requested change is complete versus partial rather than letting one positive instance dominate. The support traces repeat the same confident claim and appear dependent on one another, so they are not independent corroboration; require image-grounded localization evidence and calibrate confidence to ambiguity. No transport, schema, or dependency failure is indicated here—the disagreement is semantic classification, not missing evidence. Keep unknown for genuinely insufficient visual evidence, not as a substitute for resolving this placement distinction.
s2: The binding currently asks whether the edit was made, which lets the support node drift from its stated evidence-only role into a completion judgment. Keep it focused on whether the bowl and contents are assessable, and require the trace to localize any frog relative to the bowl interior rather than infer placement from proximity or a generic “inside” claim. The edited image shows a frog in the bowl, but also frogs on the raised lid and floor; the source has no frogs. Preserve that evidence for the downstream fulfillment check to distinguish progress from complete fulfillment—do not make this support node decide the aggregate label. Avoid treating repeated dependent claims as corroboration, and calibrate confidence to the actual visual localization. This is a semantic criterion/binding issue, not a transport, schema, or dependency failure; reserve unknown for genuinely inadequate visibility.

Do not let the bowl frog alone turn this support check into a completion judgment or erase evidence of other placements—leave progress-versus-fulfillment to the downstream evaluator. Require concrete localization rather than a generic “inside” assertion, and calibrate confidence to what the image actually resolves. This is a semantic binding/evidence issue, not a transport, schema, or dependency failure; use unknown only when visibility genuinely prevents assessment."}
